items.usageNote: Sino-Korean numbers are used for prices, phone numbers, dates and minutes; 하나 is the native Korean one, used for counting items.
Sounds identical to the number 2 and to the word for "tooth" and "this"; context makes it clear. Use 둘 (native Korean) when counting objects or people.
Used for phone numbers, dates, money, and floors; use native 셋 or 세 when counting objects.
Sino-Korean 사 is avoided in some contexts because it sounds like 死 (death), so 4th floor is often labeled F in elevators.
Use 오 for phone numbers, dates, money, and floors; use native 다섯 when counting items or people.
In dates and phone numbers 6 is 육, but when counting objects or saying age you use the native form 여섯. In compounds like 6월 it is pronounced 유월.
Sometimes said as 칠 and 일 can sound alike over the phone, so 일 is often pronounced 'il' and 칠 stays distinct as 'chil'; for clarity people may say 칠 clearly with a stressed ch.
여덟 is the native Korean eight, used for counting things and for age; 팔 is used for dates, money, phone numbers, and floors.
Sino-Korean 구 is used for phone numbers, dates, and prices; the native word 아홉 is used for counting items and age.
Use 십 for phone numbers, dates, money and minutes; the native Korean 열 is used for counting items and hours.
Pronounced "sibil": the ㅂ of 십 links to the vowel of 일. Use it for dates (11일), minutes, and addresses; use native 열한 for counting things (열한 개).
Pronounced 'sibi' (the ㅂ links to the next syllable); use 십이 for dates, months (십이월), phone numbers and money, but 열두 before counters like 개 or 명.
Used for phone numbers, addresses, dates and floors; for counting things or age, use the native number 열세 instead.
Sino-Korean 14 is used for phone numbers, dates, minutes, and addresses; for counting things or age, use native Korean 열네 instead.
The ㅂ in 십 is pronounced like a soft 'b' before 오, so it sounds like 'sibo', not 'sip-o'. Native Korean 열다섯 is used for counting things, not for this system.
Pronounced "sibyuk" (not "sipyuk"); ㅂ is voiced between the two syllables, and some speakers also say "simnyuk".
Use 십칠 for phone numbers, dates, room numbers and money; for counting things or saying age, use native Korean 열일곱 instead.

Heads up: 십팔 is pronounced close to a common swear word when said fast, so Koreans often say it carefully or use a different number when joking around, but it's totally normal for ages, dates, and counting.
Used for ages in some contexts like dates, addresses, phone numbers, and money; for counting people or things with a counter, Korean uses native numbers (열아홉) instead.
Use 이십 for dates, money, phone numbers, and minutes; for counting items or age, native Korean 스물 (seumul) is used instead.
Use this for dates, phone numbers, money, and floors; for age or counting items, use native Korean "스물한" (seumulhan) instead.
Use this Sino-Korean form for things like dates, minutes, addresses, and phone numbers; for age or counting items, use the native form 스물두 (seumuldu) instead.
Use this Sino-Korean form for things like phone numbers, dates, addresses, and money; for counting items or giving age, Korean uses 스물셋 instead.
Use Sino-Korean 삼십사 for things like phone numbers, addresses, dates, and money; for counting items or age you'd use the native form 서른네.
Use this Sino-Korean form for things like phone numbers, addresses, minutes, and prices; for age, you'd use the native form 마흔다섯.
After 십, 육 is pronounced 'nyuk' in some compounds, but in plain counting it is said 'yuk', so 56 sounds like 'o-sip-yuk' (often heard as 'osimnyuk').
Pronounced "yuk-sip-chil"; in fast speech 육십 often sounds like "yuk-ssip", and 칠 is sometimes said as 일곱-free Sino form only, so don't swap in native 일곱.
Commonly used for ages in the seventies, addresses, phone numbers, and prices; 78 pronounced as 'chilsippal' with the 'sip' and 'pal' blending.
Use for phone numbers, prices, room numbers, and ages in the formal sense; for age in everyday speech, native Korean numbers like 여든아홉 are used.
Say 백 on its own for 100; don't add 일 before it (일백 sounds unnatural).
Korean drops the 일 before 백, so say 백십오, not 일백십오; the ㅂ in 십 links to 오 and sounds like 'sibo'.
Commonly used for prices in won, e.g. 이백오십 원, and for amounts in grams or milliliters.
Korean doesn't say 'one hundred' as 일백; 100 is just 백, but 200 needs the 이 in front.
Korean doesn't say 'one' before hundred, so 100 is just 백, and 500 is 오백. Often used for prices, e.g. 오백 원 (500 won).
Korean doesn't use a word for 'and' here; for prices, add 원 (won) after it: 칠백오십 원.
Say 천, not 일천, for 1,000; 일 is normally dropped before 천, 백, and 십 (but kept before 만 as in 일만).
Korean drops the "one" before hundreds and thousands, but here both 이 and 오 are needed; in prices, add 원 (이천오백 원 = 2,500 won).
When talking about prices, Koreans usually add 원 (won) after it, and drop the 일 from 천 and 만 (so 1,000 is just 천, not 일천).
Before a counter it becomes 한, as in 한 개 (one item), 한 명 (one person), or 한 시 (one o'clock).
Before a counter it shortens to 두, as in 두 명 (two people) or 두 시 (two o'clock).
Before a counter it becomes 세, as in 세 시 (three o'clock) or 세 명 (three people).
Before a counter it becomes 네, as in 네 명 (four people) or 네 시 (four o'clock).
Used with counters, e.g. 다섯 명 (daseot myeong) means five people, and 다섯 시 (daseot si) means five o'clock.
Used before a counter, e.g. 여섯 시 (yeoseot si) means six o'clock, and 여섯 명 (yeoseot myeong) means six people.
Used with counters, e.g. 일곱 시 (seven o'clock) or 일곱 명 (seven people); use 칠 for dates, phone numbers and money.
Used with counters, e.g. 여덟 시 (yeodeol si) means eight o'clock, and 여덟 명 (yeodeol myeong) means eight people.
Used with counters, e.g. 아홉 시 (nine o'clock) or 아홉 명 (nine people); before a counter it stays 아홉, unlike 하나 → 한.
Used before a counter, e.g. 열 명 (yeol myeong) means ten people, and 열 시 (yeol si) means ten o'clock.
Before a counter it becomes 열한: 열한 시 (11 o'clock), 열한 명 (11 people), 열한 살 (11 years old).
Before a counter it becomes 열두, as in 열두 시 (twelve o'clock) or 열두 명 (twelve people).
Before a counter it becomes 열세, e.g. 열세 시 (13 o'clock is usually said 오후 한 시, so use 열세 명 for thirteen people or 열세 살 for thirteen years old).
Before a counter it becomes 열네, e.g. 열네 명 (fourteen people) or 열네 살 (fourteen years old).
Before a counter it becomes 열다섯, as in 열다섯 살 (fifteen years old) or 열다섯 명 (fifteen people); for the hour, 열다섯 시 isn't used, so say 오후 세 시 or 열다섯 시 only in 24-hour style.
Before a counter it becomes 열여섯 as is, e.g. 열여섯 살 (sixteen years old) or 열여섯 명 (sixteen people).
Before a counter it becomes 열일곱 살 (seventeen years old) or 열일곱 명 (seventeen people); 열일곱 시 is rarely used, as clock hours only go up to 열두 시 in native numbers.
Before a counter it becomes 열여덟 살 (yeolyeodeol sal) for age 18, and 열여덟 명 means eighteen people.
Used for age: 열아홉 살 (yeolahop sal) means nineteen years old; before a counter it stays 열아홉, e.g. 열아홉 명 for nineteen people.
Before a counter it becomes 스무, e.g. 스무 살 (seumu sal) means twenty years old.
Used for age, e.g. 서른 살 (seoreun sal) means thirty years old; before a counter it stays 서른, e.g. 서른 명 (thirty people). Note that 30 as an hour is not used.
Often used for age, e.g. 마흔 살 (maheun sal) means forty years old; 마흔 명 is forty people.
Used with counters, e.g. 쉰 살 (fifty years old) or 쉰 명 (fifty people); for 50 in other contexts like prices or phone numbers, use 오십.
The 월 comes from the Chinese character for moon (月), which is why Monday is the 'moon day'.
The 화 comes from 불 (fire), the element tied to Tuesday in the East Asian day-naming system.
The 수 comes from 水 (water), the Korean name for the planet Mercury, so 수요일 literally means 'water day'.
The 목 comes from 나무 (wood), one of the five elements the Korean weekdays are named after.
Colloquially, 불금 (bulgeum, 'fiery Friday') refers to a Friday night out, as the weekend begins.
The 토 comes from 토성 (Saturn, 'earth star'), so the day name literally ties to the earth element.
The 일 is Sino-Korean for "sun" (日), the same character as in 일본 (Japan, "sun origin"), so don't confuse it with the number 일 (one).
Use 이번 주말 for "this weekend" and 주말에 for "on the weekend."
Starts a new sentence or clause, e.g. 커피 마셨어요. 그리고 빵도 먹었어요. [I had coffee. And I also ate bread.] To join nouns, use 하고 or 와/과 instead.
Example: 커피 마실래요, 아니면 차 마실래요? [Do you want to drink coffee, or tea?]
Example: 맛있어요. 하지만 비싸요. [It's delicious. But it's expensive.] 하지만 starts a new sentence; in speech, 근데 is more casual.
Example: 만약 비가 오면 집에 있을 거예요. [If it rains, I'll stay home.] It usually pairs with -(으)면 on the verb.
Example: 왜냐하면 너무 피곤해요. [Because I'm so tired.] In everyday speech Koreans usually attach -아서/어서 to the verb instead of starting with 왜냐하면.
Example: 비가 왔어요. 그래서 집에 있었어요. [It rained, so I stayed home.]
Attach to a verb stem: 집에 가면 전화할게요. [When I get home, I'll call you.]
Example: 밥 먹고 그리고 나서 커피 마셔요. [I eat, and then I drink coffee.]
Example: 저도 또 갈래요. [I want to go too/again.] Use 도 after a noun for "also" (저도 = me too); 또 more often means "again" or "in addition".
Example: 먹기 전에 손을 씻어요. (I wash my hands before eating.)
Example: 식사 후에 커피 마셔요. [We drink coffee after the meal.] For a following clause, 다음에 or -(으)ㄴ 후에 is common; casually 뒤에 or 다음에 also works.
Example: 뭐 먹어요? [What are you eating? / What shall we eat?] 무엇 is the formal written form; in speech 뭐 is the norm.
Example: 누구예요? [Who is it?]
Example: 화장실이 어디예요? [Where is the restroom?]
Example: 언제 만나요? [When shall we meet?]
Example: 왜 늦었어요? [Why were you late?]
Example: 거기에 어떻게 가요? (eogi-e eotteoke gayo?) [How do I get there?]
Always goes before a noun, e.g. 어느 나라 사람이에요? (Which country are you from?)
Example: 이거 얼마예요? [How much is this?]
Example: 몇 개 필요하세요? [How many do you need?]. Use 몇 plus the right counter, e.g. 몇 명 for people.
이제 means "now" as a turning point ("from now on" or "by now"), while 지금 is simply the present moment.
Can be shortened to a casual 낼 in speech or texting, but 내일 is the standard form.
어저께 is a slightly longer variant of 어제 with the same meaning; both are common in speech.
나중에 means later in an open-ended sense, while 이따가 means later today, within a few hours.
곧 means soon in the near future, such as "곧 가요" (I'm going soon); 이따가 means "in a little while" and is more casual.
벌써 suggests surprise that something happened earlier than expected, while 이미 simply states that something is already done.
Used as a short reply to a question like "Have you done it yet?"; 아직 alone is casual and 아직요 keeps it polite.
아침 means early morning and also breakfast; 오전 means AM, the time before noon.
오후 covers everything from noon to evening (PM), so it is broader than English "afternoon"; 낮 refers to daytime around midday.
저녁 also means "dinner," so context tells you whether someone means the time of day or the meal.
오늘 저녁 means "this evening" and is used for earlier plans, while 오늘 밤 suggests later at night.
내주 is a more formal or written variant; in everyday speech 다음 주 is far more common.
Works as an adverb with no particle, e.g. 매일 운동해요 (I exercise every day).
